steps.body:
Same idea, new notation — and the notation is what makes it useful.

**dy = f′(x) · dx**

Read it as: *a small change dx in the input produces a change of about f′(x)·dx in the output.* The derivative is the exchange rate between the two.

That is exactly how a small measurement error propagates into the answer.

explanationVariants: V = s³ gives dV = 3s²·ds. With s = 10 and ds = 0.1, dV = 3(100)(0.1) = 30 cm³.
The true change is 10.1³ − 1000 = 30.301, so the differential is accurate to one part in a hundred.

widget.prompt: A cube's side is measured as 10 cm with an error of up to 0.1 cm. Estimate the resulting error in the VOLUME, in cm³.

numericErrors.feedback: That is the error in the SIDE. The derivative converts it: dV = 3s²·ds = 3(100)(0.1) = 30 cm³.
That is 3 × ds × 10 — a factor of s missing. dV = 3s²·ds = 300 × 0.1 = 30.
That is the volume itself, not the error in it.

steps.body: Why a 1% error in the side is a 3% error in the volume.

widget.prompt: Relative error, and why cubing triples it.

panels.title: The absolute error
panels.body: dV = 3s²·ds. With s = 10 and ds = 0.1 that is 30 cm³ — which sounds enormous next to a 0.1 cm error in the side.

panels.title: The relative error
panels.body: But the volume itself is 1000. So dV/V = 30/1000 = 3%, while the side's relative error is 0.1/10 = 1%. Relative errors are the honest comparison.

panels.title: And that 3 is the exponent
panels.body: dV/V = 3s²·ds / s³ = 3·(ds/s). The relative error is multiplied by THE POWER. Cubing triples it; squaring doubles it; a square root HALVES it. That is a rule worth carrying out of this course.

widget.continueFeedback: Keep going — the third panel is the reusable fact.
widget.successFeedback: Relative error is multiplied by the exponent. Cube a measurement and you triple its percentage error.

steps.body:
So there are two errors, and they answer different questions:

**Absolute error** — dV = 30 cm³. How far off, in real units.
**Relative error** — dV/V = 3%. How far off, as a proportion.

And the exponent rule: for V = sⁿ, the relative error in V is **n times** the relative error in s.

explanationVariants: A = πr² has exponent 2, so a 1% error in r gives a 2% error in the area.
dA/A = 2πr·dr / πr² = 2(dr/r). The π cancels and the exponent survives.

widget.prompt: A circle's radius is measured with a 1% error. What is the resulting percentage error in the AREA?

approxConstants.label: the percentage error in the radius

numericErrors.feedback: The area depends on r SQUARED, so the relative error doubles: 2%.
That is the rule for a CUBE (volume). An area goes with the square, so the factor is 2.

widget.explorationFeedback: Inspect the required exact-number states before checking.

explanationVariants: √s = s^(1/2), so the relative error is HALVED: a 4% error in s gives a 2% error in √s.
Roots are forgiving. That is why taking a square root of a noisy measurement is a way of quietening it.

widget.prompt: A quantity s is measured with a 4% error. What is the error in √s?

options.label: About 2% — the exponent is 1/2, so the relative error is halved.
options.feedback: Right. Roots are forgiving: taking a square root of a noisy measurement quietens the noise.

options.label: Also 4%.
options.feedback: Only if the exponent were 1. Here it is 1/2, so the relative error is halved.

options.label: 8% — the error doubles.
options.feedback: Doubling happens when you SQUARE. A square root does the opposite.
That would be squaring the error itself, which is not what the rule says. Multiply the relative error by the EXPONENT, which is 1/2.

hints: Work backwards. You want dV/V ≤ 3%, and dV/V = 3(ds/s).
So 3(ds/s) ≤ 0.03, giving ds/s ≤ 0.01 — a 1% tolerance on the side.
The side is 10 cm, so ds ≤ 0.01 × 10.
explanationVariants: 3(ds/s) ≤ 0.03 gives ds/s ≤ 1%, and with s = 10 that means ds ≤ 0.1 cm.
This is how engineering tolerances are actually set: decide what error you can live with in the OUTPUT, and the exponent rule tells you how precisely you must measure the input.

widget.prompt: A cube's volume must be accurate to within 3%. How precisely must the 10 cm side be measured, in cm?

approxConstants.label: the allowed percentage error in volume

numericErrors.feedback: That is 3% of the SIDE. But the volume's error is THREE times the side's, so the side must be measured to 1%, i.e. 0.1 cm.
That is 3% written as a decimal, not a length. Apply it to s = 10 after dividing by the exponent 3.
That is 10% of the side — far too loose. It would give a 30% error in the volume.

steps.body: The derivative is an exchange rate.
takeaways: dy = f′(x)·dx — a small input change buys an output change of about f′(x) times as much.
For y = xⁿ, the RELATIVE error is multiplied by n. Cubing triples it; a square root halves it.
Run it backwards to set tolerances: decide the error you can accept in the output, and the rule tells you how precisely to measure the input.

concept.body: A small error in the input becomes an error in the output, and the derivative is the conversion factor: **dy = f′(x)·dx**. Big derivative, big amplification. That is all a differential says.

explanationVariants: The derivative 2πr is the exchange rate.

widget.prompt: A = πr². With r = 5 and dr = 0.1, estimate dA, to two decimals.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the error in the RADIUS. Multiply by the derivative 2πr = 10π ≈ 31.4 to get about 3.14.
That is the AREA itself (25π), not the error in it.
